title: Ensembles — Bagging & Random Forest
summary: Why averaging many imperfect models reduces variance, and how random forest turns that idea into a practical, hard-to-beat algorithm.

slides.markdown:
A single decision tree is unstable — retrain it on a slightly different sample and you often get a different tree. **Random forest** exploits that instability: it grows hundreds of different trees and averages their votes.

Each tree overfits its own slice of data differently, so their errors are largely uncorrelated. Averaging cancels out those independent mistakes while the shared true signal survives — you trade a single fragile model for a stable committee.

If you average `N` models whose errors are **independent** and each has variance `σ²`, the averaged prediction's variance drops to roughly `σ²/N` — the errors partially cancel instead of stacking.

The catch is "independent": if all your models are near-identical (e.g. the same tree trained on the same data), averaging buys nothing, since correlated errors don't cancel. The whole ensembling game is about deliberately **decorrelating** the models before averaging them.

slides.subTitle: Bootstrap aggregating
slides.markdown:
**Bagging** decorrelates models via the data: draw `N` random samples **with replacement** from the training set (each the same size as the original — a **bootstrap sample**), train one model per sample, then average their predictions (or majority-vote for classification).

Each bootstrap sample omits roughly a third of the original rows and duplicates others, so each tree sees a genuinely different dataset. That's enough randomness alone to meaningfully reduce variance — bagging works with any high-variance base model, not just trees.

slides.subTitle: Bagging plus feature randomness
slides.markdown:
Random forest adds a second source of randomness on top of bagging: at **each split**, instead of considering all features, it only considers a random subset (commonly `√p` of `p` features).

This matters because bagging alone still lets a few dominant features control the top split of nearly every tree, making the trees more correlated than they look. Forcing a random feature subset per split breaks that dominance, so different trees end up structurally different — the extra decorrelation is what makes random forest beat plain bagged trees.

slides.subTitle: Aggregating the votes
slides.markdown:
Every tree sees a different bootstrap sample and a different feature subset per split, then casts one vote.

![A random forest aggregating predictions across many independently-trained trees](assets/forest-aggregation.svg)

Classification takes the **majority vote**; regression averages the numeric outputs. No single tree's mistake dominates — it only sways the answer if many trees happen to agree on it.

slides.subTitle: Out-of-bag error
slides.markdown:
Because each bootstrap sample leaves out roughly 37% of rows, every training example is "out-of-bag" for some subset of trees — those trees never saw it during training.

So for each row, you can predict it using only the trees that excluded it from training, and compare to the true label. Average that over all rows and you get the **OOB error** — a validation-quality estimate of generalization performance **without holding out a separate validation set**, essentially free from the training process itself.

A forest can rank features by **importance** — commonly, how much each feature's splits reduce impurity on average across all trees, or how much OOB accuracy drops when that feature's values are randomly shuffled (**permutation importance**).

Both are genuinely useful for feature selection and sanity-checking a model — but they measure *how much a feature was used*, not causal effect, and they can mislead when features are correlated or have very different numbers of distinct values.

**The mistake:** trusting built-in Gini-based feature importance to compare a high-cardinality feature (like a customer ID or zip code) against a low-cardinality one (like a yes/no flag).

**Why it breaks:** a feature with many distinct values has more possible split points to try, so it gets more chances to look like it reduces impurity by chance alone — inflating its importance score even when it's not truly predictive.

**The fix:** prefer **permutation importance** (measured on held-out data) over built-in Gini importance when comparing features of very different cardinality.

slides.subTitle: Correlated features split importance and look individually weak
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If two features are both genuinely predictive but one shows much lower feature importance than the other, the lower one must not matter much."

**Why it's wrong:** when two features are highly correlated (say, `annual_income` and `monthly_income`), a tree only needs to pick **one** of them at each split to capture the signal — which one it happens to pick can vary tree to tree, so the true predictive value gets split across both features' importance scores instead of concentrating in either one. Each can end up looking individually mediocre even though the underlying signal they share is strong.

**Correct model:** check for correlated features before trusting individual importance scores at face value — group or cluster correlated features and look at their combined importance, or drop the redundant one and recheck, rather than concluding a feature is unimportant just because its solo score looks unremarkable.
